request.system: You are a senior clinical coder in an Australian public hospital with fifteen years of experience coding inpatient episodes in ICD-10-AM. You are careful, conservative, and you never invent a code you are not sure of the chapter for.

messages.content:
Code the episode of care below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed. Give the three-character ICD-10-AM category for the principal diagnosis.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Age: 12
Sex: Female
Date of Admission: [redacted]
Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the emergency room with intense left flank pain, which was discovered to be caused by an obstructing calculus in the left ureter and nephrolithiasis. The patient was treated with pain control medications and hydration, and subsequently referred to a nephrologist. The patient underwent a "stone risk study" and renal ultrasound, which showed multiple bilateral cysts and renal calculi. Genetic testing was performed and identified dual mutations in GANAB and PKD1genes. 
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Discharge Instructions:
-The patient should follow up with the nephrologist for further evaluation and management of the polycystic kidney disease.
-The patient should return if she experiences any further pain or symptoms.

Follow-up:
The patient will follow up with the nephrologist for further evaluation and management of the polycystic kidney disease.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
CODE: N20

The principal diagnosis is the obstructing left ureteric calculus (N20.1, Calculus of ureter), which caused the presenting left flank pain and drove the admission. The polycystic kidney disease (Q61.x) and the GANAB/PKD1 findings were identified during the investigation but did not occasion the episode, so they are secondary diagnoses.
